theory_title: The only life cover worth buying
theory_content: Term insurance pays a lump sum if you die during the policy period and nothing if you do not. That is why it is cheap: about ₹12,000 a year for ₹1 crore of cover at age 30. Endowment, ULIP and money-back policies bundle a small amount of cover with a poor investment, and cost five to ten times as much per rupee of protection. Buy protection and investment separately, always.

theory_title: Working out the number rather than guessing
theory_content: A workable figure is ten to fifteen times annual income, plus outstanding loans, minus existing savings. Someone earning ₹12 lakh with a ₹40 lakh home loan and ₹10 lakh saved needs roughly ₹1.5 crore. The question the number answers is: if my income stopped today, does my family keep their life and their house?

theory_title: Why policies fail when they are needed
theory_content: The commonest cause of rejection is non-disclosure — an omitted medical condition, smoking, or an existing policy. Insurers cannot contest a claim after three years under Section 45 except for fraud, but within three years they can and do. Disclose everything, even if it raises the premium. A cheaper policy that does not pay is worth nothing.

theory_title: What the policy does not say on the front page
theory_content: Look past the sum insured at three things: the waiting period for pre-existing conditions, usually two to four years; room rent limits, which cap the whole bill proportionally if you take a costlier room; and co-payment, where you pay a fixed share of every claim. A ₹10 lakh policy with a 1% room rent cap can pay far less than a ₹5 lakh policy without one.
